record.title: Cloudflare outage on November 18, 2025
record.summary: On 18 November 2025, a permissions change to a ClickHouse database cluster caused a query used to generate Cloudflare's Bot Management feature file to return duplicate rows, doubling the file's size. When this oversized file propagated across Cloudflare's network, it exceeded a hardcoded feature limit in the FL2 proxy code, causing the proxy to panic and return HTTP 5xx errors for core traffic, Workers KV, Access, Turnstile and the Dashboard. The team initially suspected a DDoS attack due to fluctuating symptoms and a coincidental status-page outage before identifying the real cause, halting propagation of the bad file, and restoring a known-good version. Core traffic was largely restored by 14:30 UTC, with all systems fully recovered by 17:06 UTC.

trigger.label: config_change
trigger.quote: we made a change at 11:05 to make this access explicit, so that users can see the metadata of these tables as well
trigger.description: A change to ClickHouse database permissions/grants, deployed at 11:05 UTC, made metadata for underlying sharded tables explicitly visible, causing a metadata query used by the Bot Management feature-file generator to return duplicate columns.

mechanism.label: crash_on_bad_input
mechanism.quote: thread fl2_worker_thread panicked: called Result::unwrap() on an Err value
mechanism.description: The Bot Management feature file, now containing duplicate rows and exceeding a hardcoded 200-feature limit, caused the FL2 proxy's Rust code to panic on an unhandled Result::unwrap() error, producing widespread HTTP 5xx errors.

detected_at.quote: The first automated test detected the issue at 11:31 and manual investigation started at 11:32.

mitigations.text: Stopped the generation and propagation of the bad Bot Management feature file and manually inserted a known-good file into the distribution queue.
Forced a restart of the core proxy after restoring the good feature file.
Implemented bypasses for Workers KV and Cloudflare Access to fall back to a prior version of the core proxy, reducing impact.
Attempted traffic manipulation and account limiting to bring Workers KV back to normal operating levels during investigation.
Scaled control plane concurrency to restore dashboard availability after a login backlog developed.

blast_radius.qualitative: Today was Cloudflare's worst outage since 2019; the majority of core traffic stopped flowing through the network.

impact_start.quote: Deployment reaches customer environments, first errors observed on customer HTTP traffic.

mitigated_at.quote: Main impact resolved. Downstream impacted services started observing reduced errors.

remediations.text: Harden ingestion of Cloudflare-generated configuration files in the same way as user-generated input.
Enable more global kill switches for features.
Eliminate the ability for core dumps or other error reports to overwhelm system resources.
Review failure modes for error conditions across all core proxy modules.

record.detection_quote: The first automated test detected the issue at 11:31 and manual investigation started at 11:32.

contributing_factors.text: There were assumptions made in the past that the metadata query would only return columns from the default database, which was no longer true after the permissions change.

Cloudflare's status page, hosted independently of Cloudflare infrastructure, coincidentally went down at the same time, leading the team to initially suspect a coordinated attack rather than an internal failure.

Significant increases in latency were caused by large amounts of CPU being consumed by debugging and observability systems that automatically enhance uncaught errors with additional debugging information.

document.title: Postmortem of database outage of January 31

record.title: Postmortem of database outage of January 31
record.summary: A spike in database load (from suspected spam and an accidental hard-delete job) caused PostgreSQL replication to the secondary to fail. While attempting to manually rebuild the secondary, an engineer intended to wipe its data directory but ran the command against the primary instead, deleting roughly 300GB of live production data. Recovery was severely hampered because the pg_dump backups had been silently failing for months (wrong PostgreSQL version), Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database hosts, and DMARC misconfiguration suppressed failure-notification emails, forcing GitLab to restore from a 6-hour-old LVM snapshot over very slow network-throttled storage. The service was down for about 18 hours and some data created between 17:20 and 00:00 UTC on January 31 was permanently lost.

trigger.label: manual_command
trigger.quote: Trying to restore the replication process, an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary. Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead.
trigger.description: While trying to rebuild the lagging PostgreSQL secondary, an engineer intended to wipe the secondary's data directory but instead ran the wipe command against the production primary database.

mechanism.label: accidental_data_deletion
mechanism.quote: The engineer terminated the process a second or two after noticing their mistake, but at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.
mechanism.description: The command removed roughly 300GB of live data from the primary database's data directory, taking the primary offline and destroying data that could not be recovered because all other backup mechanisms had also failed.

mitigations.text: Temporarily increased max_wal_senders from 3 to 32 to allow replication connections.
Reduced max_connections from 8000 to 2000 to allow PostgreSQL to restart.
Restored production database using the 6-hour-old LVM snapshot, copying data from staging to production.
Restored webhooks separately from a staging database built without the webhook-removal step.
Incremented all database sequences by 100,000 to avoid ID reuse.
Gradually re-enabled GitLab.com after restoration.

resolved_at.quote: Around 18:00 UTC we finished the final restoration procedures such as restoring the webhooks and confirming everything was operating as expected.

blast_radius.qualitative: GitLab.com was unavailable for many hours, with permanent loss of some database data; code repositories and wikis were unavailable but not lost.

contributing_factors.text: A spike in database load, suspected to be caused by spam, increased pressure on the primary.
A background job accidentally scheduled to hard-delete a GitLab employee's account (flagged for abuse) added to the load.
GitLab.com was not using WAL archiving, so the primary removed WAL segments the secondary still needed, breaking replication.
pg_basebackup's normal silent-wait behavior while waiting for the primary was not documented in engineering runbooks, causing confusion.
The pg_dump backup procedure ran on an application server without a PostgreSQL data directory, causing Omnibus to default to PostgreSQL 9.2 and pg_dump to fail against the 9.6 database.
DMARC was not enabled for cronjob failure-notification emails, so the backup failure emails were rejected and never seen.
Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers because other backup procedures were assumed sufficient.
The staging environment used slow, non-premium Azure storage throttled to ~60Mbps, making the restore extremely slow.
There was no ownership for testing the backup procedure on a regular basis.

record.time_to_mitigate_text: GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours.

document.title: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region

record.title: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region
record.summary: On October 19–20, 2025, a latent race condition in Amazon DynamoDB's automated DNS management system caused an older DNS plan to overwrite a newer one and then be deleted, leaving the regional DynamoDB endpoint with an empty DNS record and causing widespread API errors in US-EAST-1. This DynamoDB failure cascaded into EC2 instance launch failures, Network Load Balancer connection errors, and downstream impact to Lambda, ECS/EKS/Fargate, Amazon Connect, STS, IAM console sign-in, Redshift, and AWS Support Console, among other services. Engineers restored DynamoDB DNS state by 2:25 AM PDT on October 20, but recovery of EC2, NLB, and dependent services continued throughout the day, with the overall event declared resolved at 2:20 PM PDT on October 20.

mechanism.label: race_condition
mechanism.quote: The race condition involves an unlikely interaction between two of the DNS Enactors.
mechanism.description: A race condition between two independent DNS Enactor processes caused an older, stale DNS plan to overwrite a newer plan for DynamoDB's regional endpoint, and the subsequent cleanup process deleted that plan, removing all IP addresses for the endpoint and leaving the DNS management system in an inconsistent state that blocked further automated repair.

mitigations.text: Engineers applied temporary mitigations enabling some internal services to connect to DynamoDB and repaired key internal tooling.
Manual operator intervention restored DynamoDB's DNS state after the inconsistent state blocked automated updates.
Engineers throttled incoming work and began selective restarts of DWFM hosts to recover from congestive collapse.
Engineers disabled automatic health check failovers for NLB, allowing healthy nodes and targets back into service.
Engineers relaxed EC2 request throttles as launches stabilized.
Restored the internal subsystem responsible for polling SQS queues.
Throttled Lambda Event Source Mappings and asynchronous invocations to prioritize synchronous invocations.
Engineers took action to stop the Redshift replacement-workflow backlog from growing.
Re-enabled automatic DNS health check failover for NLB after EC2 recovered.

resolved_at.quote: ended at 2:20 PM PDT on October 20

blast_radius.qualitative: We know this event impacted many customers in significant ways.

quantitative.quote: Services like DynamoDB maintain hundreds of thousands of DNS records to operate a very large heterogeneous fleet of load balancers in each Region.
quantitative.metric: DNS records maintained by DynamoDB's DNS management system

impact_start.quote: the event started at 11:48 PM PDT on October 19

remediations.text: Disabled the DynamoDB DNS Planner and DNS Enactor automation worldwide.
Will fix the race condition scenario and add additional protections to prevent application of incorrect DNS plans before re-enabling automation.
Adding a velocity control mechanism to limit the capacity a single NLB can remove when health check failures cause AZ failover.
Building an additional test suite to augment scale testing, exercising the DWFM recovery workflow to identify future regressions.
Will improve the throttling mechanism in EC2 data propagation systems to rate limit incoming work based on queue size.
Took additional actions to prevent recurrence of the AWS Support Center account-metadata subsystem issue.
Will look for additional ways to avoid impact from a similar event in the future and reduce time to recovery.

contributing_factors.text: The one-time check that a plan is newer than the previously applied plan was stale due to unusually high delays in Enactor processing, so it did not prevent the older plan from overwriting the newer one.
The NLB health checking subsystem brought new EC2 instances into service before their network state had fully propagated, causing health checks to alternate between failing and healthy.
Due to the large number of droplets, DWFM's efforts to re-establish leases took too long and timed out, pushing DWFM into congestive collapse.
The DWFM congestive collapse situation had no established operational recovery procedure, requiring engineers to proceed cautiously.

document.title: 2023-03-08 Incident: Infrastructure connectivity issue affecting multiple regions | Datadog

record.title: 2023-03-08 Incident: Infrastructure connectivity issue affecting multiple regions | Datadog
record.summary: On March 8, 2023, an automatic security update to systemd was applied to VMs across five Datadog regions at the same 06:00-07:00 UTC window, causing systemd-networkd to forcibly delete routes managed by the Cilium CNI plugin on restart. This took tens of thousands of nodes offline simultaneously across US1, EU1, US3, US4, and US5, taking down the platform, APIs, monitors, and data ingestion across all services. Datadog restored web access within hours, declared services operational region by region over the following day, and fully resolved the incident on March 10 after backfilling historical data.

trigger.label: os_auto_update
trigger.quote: a security update to systemd was automatically applied to a number of VMs, which caused a latent adverse interaction in the network stack (on Ubuntu 22.04 via systemd v249) to manifest upon systemd-networkd restarting.
trigger.description: An automatic security update to systemd was applied to a number of VMs, triggering a restart of systemd-networkd that exposed a latent adverse interaction with the CNI plugin.

change_at.quote: on March 8, 2023, at 06:00 UTC, a security update to systemd was automatically applied to a number of VMs

mechanism.label: network_route_deletion
mechanism.quote: systemd-networkd forcibly deleted the routes managed by the Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin (Cilium) we use for communication between containers. This caused the affected nodes to go offline.
mechanism.description: systemd-networkd forcibly deleted the routes managed by the Cilium CNI plugin upon restart, causing the affected nodes to lose network connectivity and go offline en masse across multiple regions simultaneously.

detected_at.quote: We were first alerted to the issue by our internal monitoring, three minutes after the trigger of the first faulty upgrade (March 8, 2023, at 06:00 UTC).

mitigations.text: Focused initial efforts on restoring normal ingestion and processing for real-time telemetry data so customers could use the platform even with limited historical data access.
Switched recovery efforts to historical data that had been ingested but left unprocessed.
Provided frequent updates on the status page to keep customers apprised.
Recovered and scaled compute capacity for each region, in some cases higher than normal, to accommodate simultaneous real-time and historical data processing.
Recovered each service in parallel once compute capacity was ready.

resolved_at.quote: The incident was fully resolved on March 10, 2023, at 06:25 UTC once we had backfilled historical data.

blast_radius.qualitative: This affected tens of thousands of nodes in our fleet between 06:00 and 07:00; by 06:31 UTC, enough of our fleet was offline that the outage was visible to our customers.

quantitative.quote: This affected tens of thousands of nodes in our fleet between 06:00 and 07:00

impact_start.quote: Starting on March 8, 2023, at 06:03 UTC, we experienced an outage that affected the US1, EU1, US3, US4, and US5 Datadog regions across all services.

mitigated_at.quote: we continued our recovery efforts, and declared all services operational in all regions on March 9, 2023, 08:58 UTC.

remediations.text: Disabled the legacy security update channel across all affected regions.
Changed the configuration of systemd-networkd so it leaves the routing table unchanged upon restart.
Audited infrastructure for potential similar legacy update channels.

Highlighted the need to re-examine the choice of quorum-based control planes versus statically sharded, share-nothing data stores.

record.detection_quote: We were first alerted to the issue by our internal monitoring, three minutes after the trigger of the first faulty upgrade (March 8, 2023, at 06:00 UTC).
record.time_to_detect_text: three minutes after the trigger of the first faulty upgrade

contributing_factors.text: The base OS image used for Kubernetes had a legacy security update channel enabled, causing the systemd update to apply automatically instead of through normal change management.

The default OS update window (06:00-07:00 UTC) caused the update to apply at the exact same time across multiple regions that have no direct network connection, making the outage's scale much larger than expected.

Different cloud providers' auto-scaling logic behaved differently on unhealthy nodes (reboot vs. immediate replacement), complicating and slowing recovery, and node replacement at scale created a thundering herd against cloud provider rate limits.

Quorum-based control planes for metadata stores degrade to a full stop once quorum is lost, unlike statically sharded data stores which degrade more gracefully, complicating recovery of metadata services.

Neither a fresh nor a rebooted node exhibits the faulty behavior because systemd-networkd normally starts before CNI routing rules are installed, so no obvious test reproduced the exact failure sequence ahead of time.

record.title: October 21 post-incident analysis
record.summary: A brief network partition during routine data center maintenance triggered Orchestrator to fail over MySQL primaries from GitHub's primary US East Coast data center to the US West Coast, leaving unreplicated writes in both locations and preventing a safe failback. To preserve data integrity, GitHub kept writes on the West Coast primaries, paused webhook delivery and GitHub Pages builds, and rebuilt East Coast replicas from backup, causing 24 hours and 11 minutes of degraded service with stale/inconsistent reads, delayed webhooks, and paused Pages builds. Service was fully restored after replication caught up, a controlled failover back to the East Coast was completed, and the backlog of webhooks and Pages builds was processed.

trigger.label: infrastructure_maintenance
trigger.quote: routine maintenance work to replace failing 100G optical equipment resulted in the loss of connectivity between our US East Coast network hub and our primary US East Coast data center.
trigger.description: Routine maintenance work to replace failing 100G optical equipment caused a brief loss of connectivity between GitHub's US East Coast network hub and its primary US East Coast data center.

change_at.quote: At 22:52 UTC on October 21, routine maintenance work to replace failing 100G optical equipment resulted in the loss of connectivity between our US East Coast network hub and our primary US East Coast data center.

mechanism.label: unsafe_failover
mechanism.quote: Because the database clusters in both data centers now contained writes that were not present in the other data center, we were unable to fail the primary back over to the US East Coast data center safely.
mechanism.description: During the brief network partition, Orchestrator's automated Raft-based failover promoted West Coast MySQL replicas to primary, and once both data centers had writes not present in the other, GitHub could not safely fail back, creating prolonged data inconsistency and degraded performance.

detected_at.quote: Our internal monitoring systems began generating alerts indicating that our systems were experiencing numerous faults.

mitigations.text: Manually locked internal deployment tooling to prevent additional changes.

record.title: External Technical Root Cause Analysis — Channel File 291
record.summary: On July 19, 2024, CrowdStrike deployed two new IPC Template Instances via Channel File 291, one of which used a non-wildcard matching criterion on a 21st input field that had never been exercised before. The IPC Template Type's integration code only supplied 20 inputs to the Content Interpreter, while the Template Type Definition and Content Validator expected 21, and this mismatch had evaded all prior testing due to wildcard matching. When sensors received the new Channel File 291 content, the Content Interpreter attempted to read the nonexistent 21st input, causing an out-of-bounds memory read and a system crash (BSOD) on Windows sensors. CrowdStrike subsequently detailed multiple compounding gaps in validation, testing, and staged deployment that allowed the faulty content to reach production, and describes fixes to prevent recurrence.

mechanism.quote: the attempt to access the 21st value produced an out-of-bounds memory read beyond the end of the input data array and resulted in a system crash.
mechanism.description: The Content Interpreter attempted to read a 21st input value that the IPC Template Type's integration code never supplied (only 20 were provided), causing an out-of-bounds memory read and a Windows kernel crash.

Adding new checks in the Content Validator to ensure Template Instances do not include matching criteria over more fields than are provided to the Content Interpreter.
Modified the Content Validator to only allow wildcard matching criteria in the 21st field, preventing out-of-bounds access.
Updated Content Configuration System test procedures so every new Template Instance is tested, not just at Template Type creation.

Provided customers increased control over deployment timing/location of Rapid Response Content updates, with further granular control and release notes planned.
Engaged two independent third-party security vendors to review Falcon sensor code and the end-to-end quality process from development through deployment.

The Content Validator contained a logic error, basing its assessment on the expectation that the IPC Template Type would be provided with 21 inputs, allowing the problematic Template Instance to be sent to the Content Interpreter.
Stress testing of the IPC Template Type with a test Template Instance did not observe that the mismatched number of inputs would cause a system crash when provided to the Content Interpreter.
Template Instances were not deployed using a staged rollout, so the faulty content reached all sensors at once.

record.title: Incident details
record.summary: On June 12, 2025, an invalid automated quota policy update containing unintended blank fields was inserted into Service Control's regional Spanner tables and replicated globally within seconds. A previously unexercised code path (added May 29, 2025 without error handling or feature-flag protection) hit a null pointer when processing the blank fields, causing Service Control binaries to crash-loop globally and reject external API requests with 503 errors across Google Cloud, Workspace, and Security Operations products. Engineers rolled out a 'red-button' to disable the offending policy-serving path, restoring most regions within about 40 minutes, but us-central1 suffered a secondary herd-effect overload on its Spanner backend that took roughly 2 hours 40 minutes to fully resolve. Some downstream products, including Vertex AI Online Prediction, had residual impact lasting until 18:18 PDT.

trigger.quote: On June 12, 2025 at ~10:45am PDT, a policy change was inserted into the regional Spanner tables that Service Control uses for policies... This policy data contained unintended blank fields.

change_at.quote: On June 12, 2025 at ~10:45am PDT, a policy change was inserted into the regional Spanner tables

mechanism.label: crash_on_bad_input
mechanism.quote: Without the appropriate error handling, the null pointer caused the binary to crash... This occurred globally given each regional deployment.
mechanism.description: Service Control's newly added quota policy check code path lacked error handling and feature-flag protection, so processing the blank policy fields hit a null pointer and caused the binaries to crash-loop globally, rejecting API requests with 503 errors.

Bypassed the offending quota check to allow recovery in most regions.

record.title: Slack’s Incident on 2-22-22
record.summary: On February 22, 2022, Slack experienced a major incident in which many users could not connect to Slack because the client 'boot' process failed. The root cause was a cascading failure: a routine Consul agent upgrade rollout caused sequential churn in the memcached cache fleet, which combined with an inefficient 'scatter query' used to fetch Group Direct Message membership data during client boot, overwhelming the Vitess database tier. Responders mitigated impact by throttling client boot requests and later fixed the inefficient query and added replica reads, allowing caches to refill and service to be restored.

trigger.label: infrastructure_maintenance
trigger.quote: The PBR step on February 22 updated Consul on 25% of the fleet.
trigger.description: A percentage-based rollout (PBR) step upgrading the Consul agent binary on 25% of the fleet, followed by sequential agent restarts, caused memcached nodes to be deregistered and replaced with empty cache nodes.

change_at.quote: The PBR step on February 22 updated Consul on 25% of the fleet.

mechanism.label: cascading_overload
mechanism.quote: we hit a tipping point and entered a cascading failure scenario as we hit peak traffic for the day
mechanism.description: Cache node churn from the Consul agent restarts, combined with an inefficient scatter query for Group Direct Message membership, drove cache hit rates down and database load up in a self-reinforcing cascade that overwhelmed the Vitess datastore and broke client boot for most users.

detected_at.quote: Just after 6 a.m. Pacific Time, a number of things happened almost simultaneously: we began to receive user tickets about problems connecting to Slack, some internal users experienced problems using Slack, and a number of our engineering teams received pages or alerts about problems.

mitigations.text: Applied a restrictive throttle on client boot requests to reduce database load.
Adjusted (increased, then reduced, then increased in smaller increments) the client boot rate limit to balance recovery and load.
Paused the Consul agent restart operation that had triggered cache churn.
Modified the inefficient scatter query to read from Vitess only the data missing from memcached, rather than every shard on each miss.
Updated the query to read from Vitess replicas as well as primaries, since the GDM data is immutable and tolerant of staleness.
Slowly increased the client boot rate limit back to normal traffic levels as caches refilled, until service was fully restored.

blast_radius.qualitative: Many users were unable to connect to Slack, including the author, who was Incident Commander at the time.

impact_start.quote: Just after 6 a.m. Pacific Time, a number of things happened almost simultaneously

remediations.text: Made changes to the process for performing Consul rollouts so this failure mode should not be triggered again during upgrades.
Rolling out changes to the Mcrib control loop to avoid a similar cascading failure being triggered by network outages or partitions.
Modified the problematic scatter query to read from a table sharded by channel instead of by user.
Analyzed other cache-fronted database queries to identify other high-volume scatter queries posing similar risks.
Other longer-term projects exploring ways to increase resilience of the caching tier.

record.detection_quote: Just after 6 a.m. Pacific Time, a number of things happened almost simultaneously: we began to receive user tickets about problems connecting to Slack, some internal users experienced problems using Slack, and a number of our engineering teams received pages or alerts about problems.

contributing_factors.text: Mcrib's efficiency at detecting and replacing downed memcached instances increased churn in the cache tier and contributed to the severity of the incident.
The GDM membership query was a scatter query that, when cache was missing, had to query every shard of a keyspace sharded by user, causing superlinear database load as cache misses increased.
Client retries with exponential backoff still contributed additional load on the overloaded system.
The incident occurred during peak traffic for the day, which combined with the Consul rollout pushed the system past a tipping point.

record.title: Roblox Return to Service  | Roblox
record.summary: A Consul streaming feature enabled on a traffic-routing service, combined with a 50% increase in that service's node count the day before, triggered severe write contention in Consul under high read/write load. This, combined with a separate pathological BoltDB freelist performance issue, degraded Consul so badly that dependent systems (Nomad, Vault, service discovery) failed, taking down the entire Roblox platform for 73 hours from October 28 to October 31, 2021. Engineers went through multiple failed diagnosis and remediation attempts (hardware replacement, cluster reset, load reduction, core-count changes) before identifying and disabling the streaming feature, then carefully restored caching and other services and ramped player traffic back up via DNS steering.

trigger.label: config_change
trigger.quote: On October 27th at 14:00, one day before the outage, we enabled this feature on a backend service that is responsible for traffic routing. As part of this rollout, in order to prepare for the increased traffic we typically see at the end of the year, we also increased the number of nodes supporting traffic routing by 50%.
trigger.description: Roblox enabled the new Consul streaming feature on a backend traffic-routing service and simultaneously increased that service's node count by 50%, one day before the outage began.

change_at.quote: On October 27th at 14:00, one day before the outage, we enabled this feature on a backend service that is responsible for traffic routing.

mechanism.label: resource_contention
mechanism.quote: the design of streaming exacerbates the amount of contention on a single Go channel, which causes blocking during writes, making it significantly less efficient.
mechanism.description: The Consul streaming feature used fewer concurrency-control (Go channel) elements than long polling, causing severe write contention under very high read and write load that degraded Consul's performance and, combined with a BoltDB freelist pathology, cascaded into a full platform outage because nearly all services depend on Consul.

mitigations.text: Replaced a single Consul cluster node suspected of degraded hardware performance
Replaced all Consul cluster nodes with new, more powerful (128-core, NVMe) machines
Shut down the entire Consul cluster and reset its state from an earlier snapshot, using iptables to block traffic during recovery
Reduced Consul usage by scaling down service instance counts and decreasing health check frequency, then reintroduced load gradually
Reverted Consul cluster back to 64-core servers
Disabled the Consul streaming feature across all Consul systems
Worked around the slow-leader problem by preventing problematic Consul leaders from staying elected
Redeployed the caching system to restore it to a healthy state
Used DNS steering to gradually ramp up player access in ~10% increments

resolved_at.quote: At 16:45 Sunday, 73 hours after the start of the outage, 100% of players were given access and Roblox was fully operational.

blast_radius.qualitative: A full platform outage lasting 73 hours affecting all Roblox players, though the document states there was no user data loss or unauthorized data access.

quantitative.quote: Roblox experienced a 73-hour outage.
At 16:35, the number of online players dropped to 50% of normal.
Fifty million players regularly use Roblox every day

impact_start.quote: At 16:35, the number of online players dropped to 50% of normal.

remediations.text: Removed the circular dependency between telemetry systems and Consul
Extended telemetry systems for better visibility into Consul/BoltDB performance and added targeted alerts
Built an additional geographically distinct data center and are working toward multiple availability zones
Split some critical services into their own dedicated Consul clusters to reduce load
Migrating data stored directly in Consul's KV store to more appropriate storage systems
Deleted a large amount of obsolete KV data, improving Consul performance
Deploying a new version of Consul that replaces BoltDB with bbolt to eliminate unbounded freelist growth
Redesigned cache deployment mechanisms to allow faster bootstrapping from a standing start
Identified Nomad enhancements to ease turning up large jobs after long unavailability, to be deployed in next Nomad upgrade
Developed and deployed mechanisms for faster machine configuration changes
Plan to carefully reintroduce streaming once a new implementation is tested at scale

record.summary: A Consul streaming feature enabled on a high-traffic backend service, combined with a 50% increase in nodes for that service, triggered severe lock contention in Consul under Roblox's high read/write load. Because Consul was a single point of failure for service discovery, Nomad, and Vault, this cascaded into a full 73-hour platform outage from October 28 to 31, 2021. A separate, unrelated pathological BoltDB freelist performance issue in Consul's Raft log storage compounded diagnosis difficulty. Roblox and HashiCorp engineers eventually disabled streaming and worked around slow leaders to restore Consul, then rebuilt caches and gradually reopened access to players.

trigger.label: config_change
trigger.quote: On October 27th at 14:00, one day before the outage, we enabled this feature on a backend service that is responsible for traffic routing. As part of this rollout... we also increased the number of nodes supporting traffic routing by 50%.
trigger.description: One day before the outage, Roblox enabled the new Consul streaming feature on a backend traffic-routing service and simultaneously increased that service's node count by 50% ahead of anticipated end-of-year traffic.

change_at.quote: On October 27th at 14:00, one day before the outage, we enabled this feature on a backend service that is responsible for traffic routing.

mechanism.label: resource_contention
mechanism.quote: the design of streaming exacerbates the amount of contention on a single Go channel, which causes blocking during writes, making it significantly less efficient.
mechanism.description: The Consul streaming feature relied on fewer Go channels for concurrency control than long polling, so under very high simultaneous read and write load it caused severe contention on a single Go channel, blocking writes and driving Consul KV write latency far above normal; since Consul was a single point of failure for service discovery, Nomad, and Vault, this cascaded into a complete platform outage.

mitigations.text: Replaced Consul cluster nodes with new, more powerful hardware (twice, including 128-core machines).
Shut down the Consul cluster and reset its state from a snapshot, using iptables to control traffic during the reset.
Scaled down non-essential Consul usage and reduced health check frequency to systematically reintroduce load.
Reverted Consul cluster hardware from 128-core back to 64-core servers.
Disabled the Consul streaming feature across all systems, which lowered KV write latency back to normal.
Worked around the slow-leader problem by preventing problematic Consul leaders from staying elected.
Redeployed and repaired the caching system to restore a healthy state.
Used DNS steering to gradually ramp player access back up in roughly 10% increments while monitoring stability.

resolved_at.quote: At 16:45 Sunday, 73 hours after the start of the outage, 100% of players were given access and Roblox was fully operational.

blast_radius.qualitative: A 73-hour, largely full-platform outage affecting Roblox's tens of millions of daily players, with online player counts dropping sharply before the system became completely unavailable.

quantitative.quote: At 16:35, the number of online players dropped to 50% of normal.
Starting October 28th and fully resolving on October 31st, Roblox experienced a 73-hour outage.
Fifty million players regularly use Roblox every day

impact_start.quote: At 16:35, the number of online players dropped to 50% of normal.

mitigated_at.quote: At 16:45 Sunday, 73 hours after the start of the outage, 100% of players were given access and Roblox was fully operational.

remediations.text: Removed the circular dependency between telemetry systems and Consul so monitoring works even when Consul is unhealthy.
Extended telemetry systems for better visibility into Consul and BoltDB performance, with targeted alerts for warning signs.
Building out an additional, geographically distinct data center and working toward multiple availability zones.
Split some critical services into their own dedicated Consul clusters to reduce load on the central cluster.
Migrating data stored directly in Consul's KV store to more appropriate storage systems.
Deleted obsolete KV data, improving Consul performance.
Working with HashiCorp to deploy a new Consul version replacing BoltDB with bbolt, to be completed in Q1.
Developing new tools and processes, including redesigned cache deployment mechanisms, to make bootstrapping more automated and less error-prone.
Identified Nomad enhancements with HashiCorp to ease turning up large jobs after long unavailability, to be deployed in the next Nomad upgrade later that month.
Developed and deployed mechanisms for faster machine configuration changes.
Plan to carefully reintroduce the streaming feature once a new implementation has been tested at scale.

record.detection_quote: On the afternoon of October 28th, Vault performance was degraded and a single Consul server had high CPU load. Roblox engineers began to investigate.

contributing_factors.text: A single Consul cluster supporting multiple workloads exacerbated the impact of these issues.
Our particular load conditions triggered a pathological performance issue in BoltDB, used within Consul to manage write-ahead-logs for leader election and data replication.
Critical monitoring systems that would have provided better visibility into the cause of the outage relied on affected systems, such as Consul, which severely hampered the triage process.
Higher core-count (128-core) dual-socket NUMA servers worsened contention on shared resources compared to the original hardware.

document.title: February 8th, 2019 - Prow responding slow & Partial outage

record.title: February 8th, 2019 - Prow responding slow & Partial outage
record.summary: A Prow client refactor deployed via an auto-generated version bump PR caused Prow to stop respecting a literal 'default' cluster alias in the build-cluster secret, so all test job workloads were scheduled onto the service cluster instead of the build cluster. Jobs scheduled there could not start due to missing credentials/volumes, and the resulting resource exhaustion made all other Prow controllers extremely slow and largely unusable. Engineers noticed the slowdown, investigated via Slack and cluster metrics, rolled back the deploy, and eventually identified and fixed the underlying alias bug, restoring healthy operation.

trigger.label: code_deploy
trigger.quote: Prow's auto-generated bump PR is merged (https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/11172), triggering a deploy. And Prow start to schedule workloads onto service cluster.
trigger.description: An auto-generated Prow version bump PR (#11172) was merged and deployed, introducing a client refactor that no longer respected the literal 'default' cluster alias.

change_at.quote: [13:20] Prow's auto-generated bump PR is merged (https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/11172), triggering a deploy.

mechanism.label: misrouting_due_to_config_bug
mechanism.quote: Our build-cluster secret literally defines a "default" cluster alias which points to our build cluster, which is not respected by the new client refactor, and by default prow schedules all workloads into the service cluster
mechanism.description: A client refactor failed to respect the build-cluster secret's literal 'default' cluster alias, so Prow scheduled all test job workloads onto the service cluster (the default alias target) instead of the build cluster, causing jobs to fail to start and the service cluster to run out of resources, which in turn made all other Prow controllers extremely slow.

mitigations.text: Rolled Prow back to v20190206-b01b288 (before the prow bump)
Cleaned up all the pods & prowjobs in the service cluster
Deployed the revert manually via kubectl apply due to missing deploy permission
Rolled Prow back to v20190125-2aca69d, before the bug was introduced
Cleaned up all wrong pods and prowjobs again and confirmed Prow healthy
